screenshots.title: the admin page came back
screenshots.context: the admin page came back the returned html names the admin dashboard. the request had no login cookie. i confirmed access to the page html. private data and admin actions need separate tests. both saved requests contain the payload, so a matching request without that header is still needed as a clean baseline. why it worked next.js used x-middleware-subrequest to track internal middleware calls. the vulnerable version accepted a value supplied by an external client. the payload repeats the middleware name five times. that reaches the recursion limit and makes the server skip middleware to avoid running it again. when the session check lives only there, the page can render without that check. why the controls let it through the first 403 shows that one request was blocked. i changed the host and added headers in the same step, so the captures do not tell us which change removed that block. the exploit header was present in both attempts, and the second attempt got through. the successful response shows that an external client could still supply the internal control value. a waf or suricata rule could block this header, but the checks in this setup allowed the successful request to reach next.js. suricata needs to see the traffic and have a matching drop rule running inline to stop it. dlp sees the response content it is configured to inspect; it does not verify the user's right to open the page. docker network isolation still allows the intended web connection. wazuh needs relevant events and rules to flag the behavior. these screenshots do not establish whether monitoring raised an alert.

screenshots.title: the user list came back
screenshots.context: the user list came back the xml response contains seven user entries. the account names shown are synthetic test data. this confirms unauthenticated access to the user list. the known cve can also allow admin actions, but these screenshots do not show an account being created or a server takeover. why it worked the vulnerable handler accepted a jsp destination from the request. the outer path entered teamcity's error handling, then the jsp value made it process a different resource internally. the ;.jsp suffix passed the handler's filename check while the destination still resolved to the rest api. the normal login check did not protect that alternate route. why the controls let it through the result points to a gap in the rules for teamcity's internal routing. the waf could inspect the query string, but the rules in this setup let the request through. checking for common attack patterns did not stop the application from serving a protected api. suricata needs to see the traffic and have a matching drop rule running inline to stop it. wazuh needs the proxy and teamcity events plus rules for the behavior. the screenshots do not show whether either raised an alert. dlp would need a policy that recognizes and blocks this output. here the user list came back as an ordinary xml response. docker isolation can restrict connections between services, but this request used an allowed web connection. the application still needed to enforce login.

screenshots.title: the command payload
screenshots.context: cve-2023-46604 / openwire activemq remote code execution i sent a crafted openwire packet to the broker listener. it made activemq load an xml payload from the payload server and run commands from it. the small payload below runs id and whoami, then writes both results to /tmp/scl-whoami.txt. the command payload the result i removed the previous proof file, sent the trigger to 127.0.0.1:16116, then read the file from the broker container. the supplied capture shows uid 0 and root inside the broker container. docker exec is used to read the proof file; the exploit enters through openwire. this demonstrates command execution in the container, not access to the docker host.

screenshots.title: the result
screenshots.context: cve-2023-46604 / openwire activemq remote code execution i sent a crafted openwire packet to the broker listener. it made activemq load an xml payload from the payload server and run commands from it. the small payload below runs id and whoami, then writes both results to /tmp/scl-whoami.txt. the command payload the result i removed the previous proof file, sent the trigger to 127.0.0.1:16116, then read the file from the broker container. the supplied capture shows uid 0 and root inside the broker container. docker exec is used to read the proof file; the exploit enters through openwire. this demonstrates command execution in the container, not access to the docker host.

screenshots.title: why it worked
screenshots.context: why it worked the vulnerable openwire decoder expected an exception type but did not first check that the supplied class was a throwable. that allowed a spring context class to be created with an xml url as its argument. spring loads the xml and creates its configured objects. this xml creates a processbuilder and calls start, which runs the shell commands with the broker process's permissions. the vendor fix checks the class type before creating the object. why the controls did not stop it the entry point is binary openwire over tcp. http waf rules cannot inspect that frame as a web request. protecting the web console leaves the broker listener needing its own network restrictions and protocol-aware inspection. suricata can detect the crafted traffic or the xml download when it sees the flow and has a matching rule. stopping it also requires inline drop enforcement. wazuh can alert on broker, network and process events, but the capture contains no sensor logs to show whether alerts were raised. the small payload writes a local file, so it does not test dlp. the supplied full-chain xml is designed to find a token, fetch recognized and unrecognized documents, and send them through the egress gateway. the screenshot provides no transfer results or dlp decisions.

screenshots.context: shared platform authentication / july 2025 base44 / private access wiz registered for a private sso application using its public app id. the researchers completed email verification and gained access despite the intended restriction. [4] base44 wiz / published verification response [4] step what happened security decision that failed app id publicly available not a secret credential registration outsider registered and verified private-app policy bypassed access new account gained entry email verification was not approved membership why it worked the shared authentication flow omitted the app's privacy policy. customer apps inherited that platform decision. [4] wix fixed the issue within 24 hours of the july 9 report, and wiz verified the fix. wix reported no evidence of prior abuse. this case establishes a platform authentication flaw; it does not establish that ai generated the vulnerable handler. [4] what i would change apply the same membership policy to registration, invitation, verification, login and account recovery. a private application should require an approved identity or invitation through every entry path. include direct api calls in the release checks. for a hosted builder, the vendor owns the shared fix. the application owner still needs to verify the privacy settings and understand what the platform actually enforces.

screenshots.title: wordpress / a ready-made form
screenshots.context: essential addons for elementor / cve-2023-32243 / 2023 wordpress / a ready-made form this is a non-ai example from a visual page-builder ecosystem. essential addons for elementor 5.4.0 through 5.7.1 let an unauthenticated caller reset another user's password when the username was known. the handler failed to validate the password-reset key. [6] essential addons patchstack / added reset-key validation [6] feature or check why it was insufficient result recovery form missing reset-key validation unauthorized password change frontend nonce available to visitors not proof of account control shared plugin same handler across sites shared vulnerability patchstack disclosed the issue in may 2023; version 5.7.2 was the first fix. wordfence then reported more than 6,900 blocked exploit attempts over five days. those are observed attack attempts, not a count of successful takeovers. [6] [7] why it matters here the site owner could add the form without writing its authentication code. security still depended on the plugin's handler, creating a dependency to review and update. what i would change keep the plugin on a maintained release with current fixes. validate the reset token for the target account before changing a password, and check permissions for other privileged actions. wordpress explicitly says nonces do not replace authentication or authorization. [15]

screenshots.title: android / shared generated code
screenshots.context: online app generators / ieee security and privacy 2018 android / shared generated code oltrogge and colleagues studied android generators and a corpus of about 2.29 million free apps. at least 11.1% were generated. seven of thirteen tested generators were susceptible to reconfiguration attacks. [8] android app generators oltrogge et al. / published finding [8] problem in the study how it could be abused where it came from unprotected configuration change modules or content app and update path unsafe webview behavior reach native features shared bridge code exposed components reach internal functionality generated android components andromo and app inventor generated code for selected modules and had fewer issues. they avoided the configuration attack described for monolithic generators. these are 2018 findings, not current-version claims. [8] why it matters here a website-to-app wrapper adds a native application around web content. that wrapper may introduce permissions, exported components and bridges the website did not have. the same template can carry those decisions into many apps. what i would change review the built apk and its backend. allow only intended web origins, reject invalid tls certificates and remove sensitive native bridges from untrusted content. limit permissions and keep access checks on the backend. [14]

screenshots.title: firebase / deployment settings
screenshots.context: mobile applications / check point research / march 2022 firebase / deployment settings check point identified 2,113 mobile applications with exposed firebase databases in a virustotal-based investigation. reported examples included private messages, credentials and location data. the researchers reached the data through the database endpoint. [9] firebase check point / example of open test-mode rules [9] the report describes developers opening database access for testing and leaving it open when releasing the app. it does not identify the affected apps as ai-generated or built with a visual builder. [9] policy what it actually proves remaining risk public reads and writes any reachable client can access data no identity or ownership boundary any signed-in user may access everything the caller has an account one customer can still reach another's data identity plus record ownership the caller is permitted to access this record also validate fields and privileged actions what i would change start with denied access, then add the operations each user needs. bind private records to the verified user id and protect ownership fields from being changed. firebase warns that requiring a login alone can still give every account access to the whole database. [13] check point's cases show the deployment problem. the same backend checks should apply whether the mobile interface was written manually, assembled with blocks or generated from a prompt.
